title: Engineering porous 2D materials for electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation in decarbonized energy systems
abstract: Abstract Porous two-dimensional (2D) materials have emerged as promising electrocatalysts for small-molecule electrooxidation, including water, alcohol, urea, and formic acid oxidation, which underpin decarbonized energy systems through hydrogen generation, chemical valorization, and pollutant removal. Their high surface area, tunable electronic properties, and enhanced mass transport enable improved catalytic activity, selectivity, and kinetics, yet challenges such as structural instability, catalyst deactivation, and limited mechanistic understanding hinder broader application. While previous studies have emphasized compositional tuning and performance evaluation, a systematic understanding of how porosity, defect engineering, and interlayer interactions regulate electrooxidation efficiency and durability across different small molecules remains insufficient. This review provides a comprehensive evaluation of porous 2D materials in small-molecule electrooxidation, focusing on structure–activity relationships and catalytic mechanisms. Special attention is given to pore architecture, surface defects, electronic configurations, and interlayer coupling in governing adsorption behavior, charge transfer, and intermediate evolution. Porous 2D materials are classified into oxides and their derivatives, hydroxides, sulfides, phosphides, carbides, nitrides, and other emerging systems, with a critical assessment of their catalytic pathways, electronic features, and electrochemical stability. By elucidating reaction-specific structure–performance correlations, this review establishes a unified framework for rational design of porous 2D electrocatalysts in small-molecule electrooxidation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Small molecule electrocatalytic oxidation reactions are crucial processes in energy conversion, environmental protection, and chemical synthesis [ 1 ]. These reactions, including water oxidation, alcohol oxidation, urea oxidation, ammonia oxidation, formic acid oxidation, aldehyde oxidation, and hydrazine oxidation, play vital roles in various applications. For instance, water oxidation is central to hydrogen production, while alcohol oxidation is a key step in fuel cell technology [ 2 ,  3 – 4 ]. Additionally, urea oxidation offers significant potential for nitrogen removal in wastewater treatment. However, the performance of conventional electrocatalysts remains limited. Noble metal catalysts, such as platinum and ruthenium, offer high catalytic activity but are hindered by their high cost and scarcity, which restrict their large-scale use [ 5 ,  6 ]. Furthermore, these catalysts are prone to surface contamination and deactivation over prolonged reactions [ 7 ]. Non-noble metal catalysts, while more cost-effective, often suffer from lower catalytic activity and stability [ 8 ,  9 ]. For example, transition metal oxides exhibit some catalytic activity but are limited by factors like scarce active sites, insufficient electronic conductivity, and poor long-term stability [ 10 ]. Moreover, the performance of these catalysts is closely tied to their microstructural design [ 11 ]. Although it is known that surface structure, electronic properties, and oxygen vacancies significantly influence catalytic efficiency, how to precisely control these factors to optimize reactions remains an unresolved challenge [ 12 ,  13 – 14 ]. The catalytic processes of electron transfer, reactant adsorption, and intermediate transformation are directly influenced by the geometry and surface characteristics of the catalyst [ 15 ]. Therefore, the key challenge in catalyst design is the ability to finely tune these structural elements to improve activity and selectivity [ 16 ]. Given these challenges, innovation in microstructural design is necessary to improve catalyst performance, particularly in terms of active site density, electronic conductivity, and long-term stability [ 17 ]. The development of new materials capable of addressing these issues is essential for advancing small molecule electrocatalytic oxidation reactions [ 18 ].

Porous two-dimensional (2D) materials exhibit significant advantages in small molecule electrocatalytic oxidation reactions due to their unique layered structure and rich porosity [ 19 ,  20 ]. Their high surface area and abundant active sites effectively increase the contact area between reactants and catalysts, enhancing adsorption and facilitating catalytic reactions [ 21 ,  22 ]. Specifically, in water oxidation reactions, the layered structure promotes the formation of oxygen vacancies on the catalyst surface, which enhances catalytic performance [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. In other small molecule oxidation reactions, the porous structure optimizes the electronic and ionic conductivity, thus improving reaction rate and selectivity [ 26 ,  27 ]. For example, in alcohol oxidation reactions, the material’s electronic density can be dynamically adjusted through the pore structure, promoting electron transfer and improving catalytic efficiency [ 28 ]. Similarly, in formic acid oxidation, defects and unique pore structures on the material surface can control intermediate formation, enabling the reaction to occur at lower potentials and significantly enhancing catalytic activity [ 29 ,  30 ]. However, despite the substantial potential of porous 2D materials, several challenges remain [ 31 ]. First, while various synthesis methods are available, issues such as uneven pore structure and imprecise size control still affect the stability and reproducibility of the catalysts [ 32 ]. Second, although the porous structure provides abundant active sites, the catalyst surface may suffer deactivation due to intermediate deposition or oxidation during prolonged reactions [ 33 ]. Therefore, improving the long-term stability and anti-contamination capability of these materials remains a significant challenge [ 34 ]. More critically, most research focuses on the macroscopic performance of catalysts, with insufficient attention to how microscopic features such as pore structure, surface defects, and electronic state influence reaction mechanisms [ 35 ]. The precise control of these microscopic factors to optimize catalytic reaction pathways and improve activity, selectivity, and stability is a key issue that needs to be addressed.

This review aims to address the critical knowledge gap between the structural characteristics of porous 2D materials and their electrocatalytic performance in small-molecule oxidation reactions, which lie at the heart of decarbonized energy systems by enabling sustainable hydrogen production, organic valorization, and pollutant remediation. By systematically analyzing representative materials and reaction mechanisms, this work reveals how microscopic features of porous 2D frameworks dictate catalytic activity, providing theoretical guidance for the rational design of high-performance electrocatalysts (Fig.  1 ). Porous 2D materials are categorized into six key classes: oxides and their derivatives, hydroxides, sulfides, phosphides, carbides and nitrides, and other emerging systems. Detailed discussions are provided on their charge transport properties, electrochemical stability, and redox pathways, with particular emphasis on how pore architecture, surface defects, and oxygen vacancies regulate intermediate binding, charge transfer, and reaction kinetics. Beyond qualitative structural advantages, hierarchical porosity establishes a quantitative structure–performance relationship by simultaneously increasing electrochemically active surface area and accelerating mass transport, wherein micro-/mesopores enhance active site exposure while interconnected porous channels shorten diffusion pathways and facilitate product removal, collectively leading to reduced overpotentials, higher current densities, and improved operational stability. Unlike conventional reviews that focus on material taxonomy and device-level performance, this study emphasizes the intrinsic structure–function correlation, highlighting the role of atomic-scale engineering in optimizing activity, selectivity, and durability across diverse reaction environments. Persistent challenges such as mechanistic ambiguity, electrochemical degradation, and performance decay under dynamic operational conditions are critically analyzed, and forward-looking strategies are proposed to overcome these bottlenecks. Through this comprehensive examination, the review not only offers mechanistic insights into the catalytic behavior of porous 2D materials in small-molecule electrooxidation but also outlines a conceptual roadmap for accelerating next-generation electrocatalyst innovation toward net-zero carbon energy technologies.

sections.heading: Concept of electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation
paragraphs: Electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation refers to the electrochemical conversion of low-molecular-weight compounds into oxidized products via external potential-driven electron transfer processes, facilitated by electrocatalysts that lower reaction energy barriers and modulate reaction pathways [ 36 ]. These reactions are critical to energy conversion, environmental remediation, and industrial chemical synthesis, encompassing applications such as water electrolysis, fuel cells, nitrogen removal, and organic electrochemical transformations [ 37 ,  38 ]. Recent advances in electrooxidation catalysis have significantly expanded the diversity of oxidizable small molecules, including alcohols, amines, urea, hydrazine, and other oxygenated species, each demanding distinct interfacial dynamics and electronic descriptors for optimal conversion (Fig.  2 ). Importantly, these electrooxidation reactions are closely associated with environmental remediation and carbon-neutral energy technologies, as they enable pollutant degradation, wastewater purification, and the sustainable production of clean fuels and value-added chemicals. Unlike thermochemical oxidation, which is often kinetically sluggish and requires high temperatures or external oxidants, electrocatalytic oxidation proceeds via controlled interfacial charge transfer at the solid-liquid interface, where the catalyst plays a pivotal role in governing the adsorption, activation, and conversion of reactants [ 39 ]. Such interfacial precision offers not only enhanced reaction efficiency but also tunable selectivity, enabling pathways that are inaccessible through conventional routes and aligning with green chemistry principles. The fundamental mechanism of these reactions typically involves multi-step proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) processes, in which the oxidation state of the reactant gradually increases through successive dehydrogenation or oxygen insertion steps, forming surface-bound intermediates before eventual desorption as final products [ 40 ,  41 – 42 ]. From a kinetic perspective, proton-coupled electron transfer plays a decisive role in governing the overall reaction rate during small-molecule electrooxidation. The simultaneous transfer of protons and electrons involves the reorganization of interfacial hydrogen-bond networks, solvation structures, and surface adsorption configurations. These coupled reorganizations require overcoming a higher activation barrier than purely electron-transfer or purely proton-transfer steps, which makes the PCET process particularly sensitive to the local catalytic environment. As a result, the efficiency of PCET directly influences the overpotential required to initiate the reaction and strongly affects the achievable current density. Improving catalytic activity therefore relies on facilitating proton transport pathways, stabilizing key surface intermediates, and optimizing the electronic structure of active sites to lower the kinetic barrier associated with the coupled transfer process. The efficiency of electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation is determined by several interrelated factors, including the catalyst’s electronic structure, which dictates the binding strength and activation energy of reaction intermediates; the density and distribution of active sites, which influence turnover frequencies and overall current densities; mass transport properties, which control the diffusion of reactants and desorption of products; and catalyst stability, which determines long-term electrochemical performance under oxidative environments [ 43 ]. A major challenge in small-molecule oxidation is the competition between desired oxidation pathways and side reactions, such as the formation of poisoning intermediates or incomplete oxidation products, which necessitates the precise tuning of catalytic active sites to optimize reaction selectivity and minimize energy losses [ 44 ]. In addition, while noble metal catalysts have traditionally been employed due to their high activity and stability, their scarcity and cost drive the search for earth-abundant alternatives with comparable or superior catalytic efficiency [ 45 ,  46 ]. Given these complexities, small-molecule oxidation reactions are highly dependent on the specific chemical nature of the reactant, the number of electron transfer steps involved, and the stability of reaction intermediates, necessitating a systematic classification based on their underlying reaction mechanisms [ 47 ,  48 ].

sections.heading: Classification of electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation
paragraphs: Electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation reactions encompass a broad range of oxidation processes, each involving distinct electron transfer pathways, reaction intermediates, and catalytic challenges [ 49 ,  50 ]. While numerous oxidation reactions can be realized electrochemically, this discussion focuses on seven widely studied types that hold significant promise for energy conversion, environmental remediation, and chemical synthesis (Fig.  3 ). These include water oxidation, alcohol oxidation, urea oxidation, ammonia oxidation, formic acid oxidation, aldehyde oxidation, and hydrazine oxidation, each of which presents unique mechanistic considerations and electrocatalyst design requirements. Understanding the fundamental principles governing these oxidation processes is crucial for optimizing catalytic efficiency, selectivity, and long-term stability.

sections.heading: Water oxidation (oxygen evolution reaction, OER)
paragraphs: Water oxidation (2H 2 O → O 2  + 4 H +  + 4e − ) is the anodic half-reaction in electrochemical water splitting, crucial for sustainable hydrogen production [ 51 ,  52 ]. As a four-electron, multi-step oxidation process, OER is inherently sluggish due to the high activation energy associated with O–O bond formation [ 53 ,  54 ]. The reaction typically follows either the adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) or the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM) [ 55 ,  56 ]. In the AEM pathway, hydroxide (*OH) or water molecules adsorb onto catalytic sites, sequentially oxidizing to *O, *OOH, and ultimately forming O 2  [ 57 ]. In contrast, the LOM pathway involves direct participation of lattice oxygen from the catalyst, enabling faster charge transfer but often leading to structural degradation [ 58 ,  59 ]. The dominance of these pathways is highly dependent on the catalyst’s electronic structure and operational environment. AEM is typically favored in catalysts with strong metal-oxygen (M-O) bonds and discrete active sites, where the high energy barrier for O-O coupling on a single metal center limits the reaction kinetics. Conversely, LOM is more likely to be triggered in systems with high metal-oxygen covalency and a high-lying O 2p band, such as high-valence transition metal oxides and highly defective structures. In these environments, the enhanced overlap between metal d-orbitals and oxygen p-orbitals facilitates the direct coupling of lattice oxygen species, thereby bypassing the scaling relationship constraints inherent to AEM, albeit at the potential cost of surface lattice stability. The key challenge in OER catalysis is reducing the overpotential required to drive the reaction while maintaining catalyst stability under harsh oxidative conditions [ 60 ,  61 ]. Noble metal oxides such as RuO 2  and IrO 2  exhibit high intrinsic OER activity due to their ability to stabilize high-valence metal-oxo species, but their scarcity and cost limit widespread use [ 62 ,  63 ]. Alternative catalysts, including transition metal oxides, perovskites, and layered double hydroxides (LDHs), offer promising activity through electronic structure tuning and defect engineering, where factors such as oxygen vacancies and cation redox activity significantly influence reaction kinetics [ 64 ,  65 ].

sections.heading: Alcohol oxidation (Methanol and ethanol oxidation reactions, MOR & EOR)
paragraphs: Alcohol oxidation plays a critical role in direct alcohol fuel cells (DAFCs), where methanol (CH 3 OH) and ethanol (C 2 H 5 OH) serve as fuels that undergo electrooxidation to generate electricity [ 66 ,  67 ]. The MOR proceeds via stepwise dehydrogenation, leading to the formation of intermediate species such as formaldehyde (*H 2 CO) and formic acid (*HCOOH), before complete oxidation to CO 2  [ 68 ,  69 ]. However, MOR suffers from CO poisoning, where strongly adsorbed CO inhibits catalytic activity, necessitating the use of Pt-based bimetallic catalysts (e.g., PtRu, PtPd) that promote CO oxidation through a bifunctional mechanism [ 70 ,  71 ]. Fundamentally, the CO-tolerance is closely governed by the electronic structure of the active sites, particularly the d-band center position. According to the d-band model, shifting the d-band center away from the Fermi level weakens the adsorption energy of CO by reducing the back-donation of electrons from the metal d-orbitals to the CO 2π antibonding orbitals. Furthermore, electronic modulation through alloying or support interactions can facilitate the adsorption of oxygenated species (OH) at lower potentials. This promotes the Langmuir-Hinshelwood reaction between adsorbed CO and OH to form CO2, thereby effectively liberating active sites and enhancing the catalyst’s steady-state activity. Similarly, the EOR follows a multi-electron pathway involving *C 2  intermediates such as acetaldehyde (*CH 3 CHO) and acetic acid (*CH 3 COOH) [ 72 ,  73 ]. Compared to MOR, EOR presents greater selectivity challenges due to competing cleavage of C–C bonds, with catalysts needing to balance high activity and full oxidation efficiency [ 74 ,  75 ]. Transition metal alloys, particularly Pd-based catalysts, demonstrate high EOR selectivity, while non-precious metal catalysts such as Ni-based systems are being explored for cost-effective alternatives [ 76 ]. This enhancement mainly originates from electronic structure modulation and bifunctional effects, where the incorporation of non-noble metals optimizes intermediate adsorption and facilitates the removal of poisoning species, thereby accelerating alcohol electrooxidation kinetics.

sections.heading: Urea oxidation reaction (UOR)
paragraphs: Urea oxidation (CO(NH 2 ) 2 + 6H 2 O → N 2  + CO 2  + 6 H +  + 6e − ) is an important anodic reaction with applications in wastewater treatment, energy conversion, and nitrogen recovery [ 77 ]. Compared to water oxidation, UOR exhibits a lower theoretical onset potential (~ 0.37 V vs. RHE), making it a promising alternative for electrochemical hydrogen production while simultaneously removing nitrogenous pollutants [ 78 ,  79 ]. The reaction involves C–N bond cleavage, followed by sequential oxidation steps leading to the formation of nitrogenous and carbonaceous intermediates [ 80 ,  81 ]. The primary pathway proceeds through hydroxyl (*OH) activation, forming species such as *NH 2 COOH, *NH 2 , *NO, and *N 2 H 4  before final conversion to N 2  and CO 2  [ 82 ,  83 ]. However, competing pathways can produce undesired byproducts like NO x  and NH 4 + , necessitating catalyst designs that enhance nitrogen selectivity. Nickel-based materials, particularly Ni(OH) 2  and NiCo 2 O 4 , are among the most effective UOR catalysts due to their intrinsic redox properties that facilitate hydroxyl adsorption and activation [ 84 ,  85 ]. The incorporation of heteroatoms such as Fe, Cu, and Mo further enhances activity by tuning electronic structure and promoting charge transfer [ 86 ,  87 ]. Structural engineering strategies, including defect introduction, oxygen vacancy creation, and nanostructure optimization, have improved catalytic performance by increasing active site density and mass transport efficiency [ 88 ,  89 – 90 ]. However, catalyst stability remains a challenge, as prolonged UOR operation can lead to electrode fouling from carbonate accumulation and metal dissolution.

sections.heading: Ammonia oxidation reaction (AOR)
paragraphs: Ammonia oxidation (NH 3  → N 2  + 3 H +  + 3e − ) is essential for nitrogen cycle management, fuel cells, and electrochemical ammonia-to-nitrogen conversion [ 91 ,  92 ]. The reaction pathway involves stepwise NH₃ dehydrogenation on the catalyst surface, forming *NH 2  and *NH intermediates before N 2  evolution [ 93 ,  94 ]. However, undesired side reactions can generate NO x  species (NO 2 − , NO 3 − ), making selectivity a major challenge [ 95 ,  96 ]. Nickel-based catalysts, particularly Ni(OH) 2  and NiFe alloys, effectively activate NH 3  via metal-N interactions while facilitating proton-coupled electron transfer [ 97 ,  98 ]. Introducing oxygen vacancies, Co or Mo dopants, and porous nanostructures enhances NH 3  adsorption, optimizes charge transfer, and promotes N 2  selectivity [ 99 ,  100 ]. Electronic structure tuning plays a crucial role in lowering NH 3  dehydrogenation barriers and stabilizing intermediates [ 101 ,  102 ]. Advanced strategies, including single-atom catalysts (SACs) and heterostructured interfaces, further improve selectivity and suppress NO x  formation. However, long-term stability remains a challenge due to catalyst poisoning or oxidation-induced degradation [ 103 ]. Future research should focus on self-regenerating catalysts, optimizing reaction conditions to suppress NO x  formation, and employing in situ characterization to gain deeper mechanistic insights.

sections.heading: Formic acid oxidation reaction (FAOR)
paragraphs: Formic acid oxidation (HCOOH → CO 2  + 2 H +  + 2e − ) is a key anodic reaction in direct formic acid fuel cells (DFAFCs) and electrochemical carbon-neutral energy systems [ 104 ]. The reaction follows two competing pathways: the direct dehydrogenation pathway (HCOOH → CO 2 ) and the indirect dehydration pathway (HCOOH → CO + H 2 O → CO 2 ), with the latter being less desirable due to CO poisoning effects [ 105 ]. The preference for the direct pathway is fundamentally governed by the surface ensemble effect and the electronic configuration of active sites. Specifically, the dehydration pathway (indirect route) typically requires contiguous metal atom ensembles to facilitate the C–O bond cleavage of HCOOH. By engineering porous 2D structures with isolated active sites or introducing heteroatom dopants, these contiguous ensembles can be effectively disrupted, thereby sterically suppressing CO formation. Furthermore, tuning the surface electronic structure can optimize the adsorption geometry of HCOOH toward a “formate” intermediate rather than a “carboxyl” species. This electronic modulation increases the energy barrier for C–O bond dissociation while lowering the barrier for the direct dehydrogenation to CO2, ensuring high catalytic selectivity and CO-tolerance. The efficiency of FAOR depends on the catalyst’s ability to suppress CO formation while promoting direct oxidation [ 106 ]. Pd-based catalysts outperform Pt-based ones by favoring the dehydrogenation pathway and minimizing CO adsorption, while alloying strategies (e.g., PdAg, PdAu, PtBi) further enhance catalytic efficiency by tuning electronic structures [ 107 ,  108 ]. Non-precious metal alternatives, such as Ni- and Co-based materials, leverage oxygen-functionalized supports and defect engineering to modulate reaction pathways. The development of porous nanostructures, single-atom catalysts, and bimetallic interfaces has further optimized active site distribution, electron transfer, and catalyst stability [ 109 ]. Despite these advances, challenges remain in maintaining long-term FAOR activity under acidic conditions, mitigating catalyst poisoning, and improving mass transport [ 110 ,  111 ]. Future research should focus on the rational design of hybrid electrocatalysts with optimized adsorption properties and in situ spectroscopic studies to guide FAOR systems for efficient and sustainable energy conversion.

sections.heading: Aldehyde oxidation reaction (AlOR)
paragraphs: Aldehyde oxidation (R–CHO + H 2 O → R–COOH + 2 H +  + 2e − ) is an important electrochemical transformation with applications in fuel cells, organic synthesis, and green oxidation technologies [ 112 ]. The reaction involves nucleophilic attack by hydroxyl (*OH) species, forming hydrated carbonyl intermediates that undergo dehydrogenation to yield carboxylates [ 113 ]. The efficiency of AlOR depends on the catalyst’s ability to stabilize intermediates and control selectivity to prevent overoxidation to CO 2  [ 114 ,  115 ]. Au-based catalysts exhibit high selectivity for partial oxidation, favoring aldehyde-to-carboxylate conversion, while Pt and Pd tend to promote deeper oxidation, necessitating precise electronic structure tuning [ 116 ]. Alloying strategies, such as AuPd or Ag-based bimetallic systems, enhance oxidation efficiency by modifying the d-band center and facilitating intermediate desorption [ 117 ]. Transition metal oxides, such as MnO 2  and Co 3 O 4 , also show promise by leveraging oxygen vacancies and lattice oxygen participation to modulate reaction kinetics [ 118 ,  119 ]. The development of porous nanostructures and single-atom catalysts has further improved oxidation performance by increasing active site exposure and optimizing charge transfer [ 120 ]. Despite these advances, challenges remain in achieving long-term catalyst stability, suppressing undesired side reactions, and improving oxidation efficiency under mild conditions [ 115 ]. Future research should focus on designing cost-effective, highly selective catalysts, employing in situ spectroscopic techniques to elucidate reaction mechanisms, and integrating AlOR into scalable electrochemical applications.

sections.heading: Hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR)
paragraphs: Hydrazine oxidation (N 2 H 4  → N 2  + 4 H +  + 4e − ) is an important anodic reaction in electrochemical energy conversion and environmental remediation, owing to its low thermodynamic oxidation potential and carbon-free reaction pathway [ 121 ]. The oxidation mechanism of hydrazine typically involves successive N–H bond cleavage steps and the formation of surface-bound *NH x  intermediates, followed by rapid N–N bond retention and nitrogen evolution. On transition metal-based catalysts, the initial deprotonation of hydrazine(N 2 H 4(ad)  →N 2 H 3 *+H + +e − )is generally identified as the rate-determining step (RDS). The electronic structure of the catalyst, specifically the d-band center position, governs the adsorption strength of these NHx intermediates. An optimized metal-nitrogen (M-N) binding energy, regulated by the electronic configuration, effectively lowers the kinetic barrier for the primary N-H bond activation while preventing the over-stabilization of intermediates that could otherwise block active sites and inhibit continuous turnover. Compared with carbon-containing small molecules, HzOR proceeds with intrinsically faster kinetics and lower activation barriers, yet its catalytic performance is highly sensitive to surface electronic structure and adsorption energetics. Noble metal catalysts such as Pt, Pd, and Ru exhibit high intrinsic activity for HzOR by efficiently stabilizing *NH x  intermediates and facilitating charge transfer [ 122 ]. Alloying strategies, including Pt-based bimetallic systems, have been employed to tune electronic properties, suppress parasitic reactions, and improve catalytic durability [ 123 ]. In parallel, transition metal-based electrocatalysts, such as Ni-, Co-, and Fe-based oxides and hydroxides, have demonstrated promising activity by leveraging surface hydroxyl species, defect engineering, and redox-active metal centers to accelerate N–H bond activation. The introduction of porous architectures and 2D heterostructured catalysts further enhances HzOR by increasing active site accessibility, improving mass transport, and enabling rapid electron delocalization across ultrathin catalytic frameworks [ 124 ]. Nevertheless, challenges remain in controlling reaction selectivity, mitigating catalyst degradation under prolonged operation, and ensuring safe and efficient integration into practical electrochemical systems. Future research should focus on the rational design of earth-abundant catalysts with optimized adsorption strength, in-depth mechanistic elucidation using operando characterization techniques, and the development of scalable HzOR platforms for sustainable energy and environmental applications.

sections.heading: Influence and advantages of porous 2D materials in electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation
Limitations of conventional nanostructured electrocatalysts in small-molecule oxidation
paragraphs: The catalytic efficiency of small-molecule electrooxidation is largely dictated by the structural characteristics of the catalyst, which govern active site density, charge transfer properties, and reactant accessibility [ 125 ]. Conventional nanostructured catalysts, including nanoparticles, nanowires, and bulk crystalline materials, have been extensively explored for electrocatalytic applications [ 126 ]. However, these structures exhibit inherent limitations that constrain their effectiveness and long-term stability in oxidation reactions. For instance, zero-dimensional (0D) nanoparticles are prone to agglomeration due to high surface energy, leading to a significant reduction in the density of exposed active sites and a consequent decline in catalytic performance over time. One-dimensional (1D) nanostructures, such as nanowires and nanotubes, exhibit improved charge transport along their longitudinal axis, yet their relatively low surface-to-volume ratio results in inefficient active site utilization [ 127 ]. Furthermore, mass transport limitations in compact nanoparticle or nanowire-based catalyst assemblies introduce diffusion barriers that hinder reactant adsorption and byproduct removal, impeding the overall reaction kinetics [ 128 ]. Additionally, conventional nanostructures often lack the necessary tunability in electronic structure, which is critical for optimizing adsorption energies, stabilizing reactive intermediates, and lowering activation barriers for oxidation reactions. The structural instability of these catalysts under operational conditions also leads to deactivation through dissolution, aggregation, or surface passivation. These fundamental challenges necessitate the development of advanced catalytic architectures that integrate high active site exposure, optimized charge transport pathways, and enhanced electrochemical durability, which are intrinsically fulfilled by porous 2D materials.

sections.heading: Structural features and advantages of porous 2D materials in small-molecule electrooxidation
paragraphs: Porous 2D materials exhibit distinctive structural and electronic attributes that make them highly advantageous for electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation [ 129 ]. Unlike conventional nanostructures, which suffer from limited active site exposure, poor charge transport, and diffusion constraints, porous 2D materials provide a unique combination of ultrahigh surface area, tunable electronic states, and efficient mass transport pathways [ 130 ]. As shown in (Fig.  4 ), the synergistic interplay of pore architecture, surface defects, electronic configurations, and interlayer coupling plays a crucial role in optimizing oxidation reaction kinetics, improving selectivity, and ensuring long-term electrochemical stability [ 131 ].

sections.heading: Pore architecture and mass transport optimization
paragraphs: The introduction of intrinsic or engineered porosity within 2D materials significantly enhances mass transport, facilitating the efficient diffusion of reactants and rapid removal of oxidation byproducts [ 132 ,  133 ]. In many small-molecule oxidation reactions, such as alcohol oxidation and UOR, the accumulation of reaction intermediates at the catalyst surface can lead to deactivation. Porous structures mitigate this issue by reducing diffusion barriers, thereby sustaining high catalytic turnover rates [ 134 ,  135 ]. Additionally, the well-defined pore networks in 2D materials promote enhanced reactant accessibility, allowing for more uniform utilization of active sites across the entire catalyst surface [ 136 ]. In systems such as FAOR, where poisoning species often inhibit catalytic activity, the presence of hierarchical porosity has been shown to minimize surface blockage by enabling continuous reactant flow and product desorption.

sections.heading: Surface defects and reactive site engineering
paragraphs: Surface defects in porous 2D materials serve as critical active centers that modulate adsorption energies and reaction pathways [ 137 ,  138 ]. Unlike bulk materials with uniform coordination environments, defect-rich 2D structures exhibit undercoordinated metal sites, edge terminations, and vacancy states that provide highly reactive centers for oxidation reactions [ 139 ,  140 ]. For example, oxygen vacancies in transition metal oxides and hydroxides have been demonstrated to significantly enhance water oxidation and alcohol oxidation by stabilizing key intermediates such as *OH, *O, and *OOH. Similarly, sulfur and phosphorus vacancies in 2D sulfides and phosphides create localized electron density variations that promote selective adsorption of reaction intermediates, thereby improving product selectivity and suppressing undesired side reactions [ 141 ]. Defect engineering also influences charge redistribution at the catalyst surface, effectively lowering activation energy barriers and accelerating reaction kinetics in multi-electron oxidation processes [ 142 ,  143 ]. sections.heading: Electronic configuration modulation for activity enhancement
paragraphs: The electronic structure of porous 2D materials plays a fundamental role in determining their catalytic efficiency. By precisely tuning d-band states, charge carrier mobility, and interfacial electronic interactions, it is possible to optimize small-molecule oxidation pathways and enhance reaction selectivity [ 144 ,  145 ]. Transition metal-based 2D materials, such as oxides, sulfides, and phosphides, exhibit tunable electronic structures that can be modified through heteroatom doping or defect engineering to regulate adsorption energies and reaction kinetics [ 146 ]. For instance, doping with elements such as Fe, Co, or Ni has been shown to induce electronic charge redistribution, thereby optimizing binding affinities for oxidation intermediates and improving catalytic turnover frequencies. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations have confirmed that bandgap narrowing and charge delocalization effects in modified 2D materials lead to increased catalytic activity by reducing the energetic penalty associated with charge transfer. Furthermore, modulating the oxidation states of active metal centers in porous 2D materials allows for dynamic control of oxidation-reduction cycles, an essential feature in reactions such as AOR and UOR, where multi-step electron transfer mechanisms dictate overall efficiency.

sections.heading: Interlayer coupling and charge transport dynamics
paragraphs: Interlayer interactions within 2D materials critically influence their electrochemical performance by governing charge transfer dynamics and mechanical stability. While conventional layered 2D materials often suffer from limited electron mobility due to interlayer van der Waals interactions, introducing controlled porosity disrupts these interactions, creating expanded interlayer spacing that enhances charge transport pathways. This effect is particularly beneficial for oxidation reactions that involve rapid electron transfer processes, such as FAOR, where minimizing charge recombination is essential for sustaining high activity. In addition, interlayer coupling in 2D heterostructures, such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) derived porous 2D materials and heterostructured oxides, enables synergistic catalytic effects that optimize reaction energetics [ 147 ]. The ability to engineer strong interfacial electronic interactions in these materials ensures rapid charge injection and enhanced durability under oxidative conditions.

sections.heading: Comparative performance pnalysis of porous 2D materials in small-molecule oxidation
paragraphs: To enable a data-driven and reaction-oriented evaluation of porous 2D materials across diverse electrocatalytic oxidation processes, Table  1  consolidates representative performance metrics, including overpotential, current density, Tafel slope, and operational stability, for a broad spectrum of small-molecule oxidation reactions, thereby providing a unified basis for comparative analysis beyond isolated material systems. Despite the unified comparison of catalytic metrics, it should be noted that the intrinsic reaction kinetics of multi-electron oxidation systems differ substantially. Reactions such as OER involve complex proton-coupled electron transfer steps and oxygen–oxygen bond formation, which typically impose higher kinetic barriers and larger overpotentials. In contrast, the electrooxidation of small organic molecules is often governed by surface dehydrogenation and intermediate adsorption–desorption processes, leading to faster apparent kinetics and higher achievable current densities. These fundamental kinetic distinctions provide an essential framework for interpreting the performance trends summarized below. For OER, which involves complex multi-electron proton-coupled steps and oxygen intermediate formation, porous 2D metal oxides, hydroxides, and their in situ reconstructed derivatives consistently exhibit moderate overpotentials in the range of approximately 280–350 mV at 10 mA cm − 2 , accompanied by relatively small Tafel slopes often below 60 mV dec − 1 , indicating that lattice oxygen participation, dynamic metal oxidation state modulation, and enhanced electrolyte accessibility within porous sheets collectively accelerate rate-determining steps [ 148 ]. In contrast, alcohol oxidation reactions such as methanol and ethanol oxidation display allowing higher current densities and mass activities on porous 2D metal sulfides, phosphides, and multimetallic nanosheets, where metallic or semi-metallic electronic structures reduce charge-transfer resistance and stabilize key carbonaceous intermediates, enabling efficient C–H activation and, in some cases, facilitated C–C bond cleavage, as reflected by substantially increased current responses and prolonged durability under alkaline conditions [ 28 ]. UOR presents a distinct kinetic landscape dominated by multistep dehydrogenation and C–N bond scission, and the compiled data reveal that porous 2D hydroxides, sulfides, and nitrides achieve markedly lowered onset potentials and sustain current densities above tens to over one hundred mA cm − 2 , underscoring the importance of abundant surface hydroxyl species, moderate adsorption strength, and continuous electron pathways in stabilizing reaction intermediates and mitigating surface poisoning [ 149 ]. For FAOR, the table highlights exceptional mass-normalized activities and long-term stability on porous 2D metal nanowire networks and alloyed nanosheets, with reported activities exceeding 10 3  mA mg − 1  and superior resistance to CO poisoning, which can be attributed to 2D electron transport, high densities of low-coordination sites, and preferential promotion of the direct dehydrogenation pathway [ 150 ]. Biomass-related oxidations, including hydroxymethylfurfural oxidation, further emphasize the structural sensitivity of reaction selectivity, where porous 2D oxides and hydroxides demonstrate enhanced stability and controlled oxidation behavior under relatively high anodic potentials, reflecting improved mass transport and uniform active site exposure. For intrinsically fast reactions such as hydrazine and AlOR, ultralow Tafel slopes, in some cases below 20 mV dec − 1 , are predominantly observed on defect-rich porous 2D multimetallic and emerging hybrid systems, indicating that abundant grain boundaries, edge sites, and electronic heterogeneity significantly reduce activation barriers and facilitate rapid electron transfer [ 151 ]. Therefore, the comparative trends demonstrate that the catalytic advantages of porous 2D materials are strongly reaction-dependent, arising from the deliberate coupling of pore architecture, electronic configuration, surface chemistry, and interfacial transport to the intrinsic mechanistic requirements of each small-molecule oxidation pathway, thereby establishing a structure–reaction–performance framework for rational catalyst design.

sections.heading: Advances in porous 2D materials for electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation
paragraphs: In electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation, porous 2D materials have attracted considerable attention due to their highly tunable electronic structures, large accessible surface areas, and unique catalytic properties [ 191 ]. Different classes of porous 2D materials exhibit distinct advantages in modulating oxidation reaction pathways, optimizing charge transfer kinetics, and enhancing structural stability under electrochemical conditions [ 192 ]. However, a deeper understanding of their structure–performance relationships remains essential for advancing catalyst design. The following sections systematically explore porous 2D metal oxides, hydroxides, sulfides, phosphides, carbides, nitrides, and other emerging porous 2D materials, providing insights into their catalytic mechanisms, structural advantages, and recent developments. Through this analysis, a comprehensive framework is established to guide the rational design of next-generation porous 2D electrocatalysts for small-molecule oxidation. Notably, although the reconstruction pathways differ among catalyst systems, the process commonly leads to the formation of surface oxyhydroxide species that serve as the catalytically active phases under electrooxidation conditions. From a structure–performance perspective, the trends summarized in Sect.   4  can be rationalized by the complementary roles of the material classes discussed in Sect.   3 . Porous 2D oxides and hydroxides usually provide stronger structural robustness and more favorable hydroxyl-assisted surface chemistry, which is advantageous for reactions requiring sustained anodic operation. However, their relatively lower intrinsic conductivity and stronger binding to oxygenated species can slow charge transfer and intermediate turnover, particularly under high-current UOR conditions. By contrast, porous 2D sulfides and phosphides generally offer faster electron transport and more flexible surface electronic structures, which facilitate intermediate conversion and often lead to lower kinetic barriers in UOR and alcohol oxidation. Their main limitation is that they are more prone to surface oxidation or reconstruction during prolonged operation. Carbides, nitrides, and selected hybrid systems often sit between these two extremes, combining improved conductivity with better structural tolerance. This comparison clarifies why different porous 2D classes outperform one another only under specific reaction environments, rather than following a universal ranking.

sections.heading: Porous 2D metal oxides and their derivatives
paragraphs: Porous 2D metal oxides exhibit exceptional catalytic properties in small-molecule oxidation due to their highly tunable electronic structures, abundant surface oxygen functionalities, and redox-active metal centers. Unlike other material classes, metal oxides possess strong metal-oxygen covalency, which enables efficient charge delocalization and facilitates electron transfer during oxidation reactions [ 193 ,  194 ]. The d-band states of transition metal oxides can be precisely modulated to optimize the binding strength of key reaction intermediates, allowing for controlled adsorption and desorption processes that minimize energy barriers in oxidation pathways [ 195 ]. Furthermore, the presence of oxygen vacancies and lattice distortions in porous 2D metal oxides plays a critical role in enhancing their catalytic activity, as these defects introduce localized electronic states that act as additional charge transfer channels and reactive sites. Oxygen vacancies, in particular, serve as active centers for the adsorption and activation of reactant molecules, lowering activation energies and accelerating reaction kinetics [ 196 ]. The open-framework structure of porous 2D metal oxides further improves mass transport and intermediate diffusion, mitigating issues related to reactant accumulation and byproduct poisoning. Additionally, their strong hydrophilic nature and high proton affinity enable rapid proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET), which is essential for oxidation processes involving multi-step protonation and deprotonation events. The adaptability of metal oxides under electrochemical conditions also leads to the formation of metastable phases with enhanced reactivity, as in situ transformations can generate oxyhydroxide layers that act as highly active catalytic interfaces [ 197 ]. These unique structural and electronic properties collectively enable porous 2D metal oxides to effectively catalyze small-molecule oxidation reactions, offering a platform for tailoring adsorption energies, stabilizing reaction intermediates, and optimizing charge transfer dynamics to achieve superior electrocatalytic performance [ 198 ].

Building on these intrinsic advantages, recent efforts show that targeted microstructural and phase engineering can effectively translate the favorable properties of porous 2D metal oxides into enhanced electrocatalytic activity and stability. He et al. developed a grain-boundary engineering approach to enhance durability, wherein they synthesized grain-boundary-rich ultrathin porous RuO 2  nanosheets (GB-RuO 2 ) through a salt-assisted recrystallization process [ 152 ]. The presence of grain boundaries disrupts the local symmetry of bulk RuO 2 , giving rise to tensile strain and unsaturated Ru coordination environments. These structural distortions modulate the Ru–O bonding characteristics and the local electronic structure, thereby influencing the adsorption behavior of oxygenated intermediates and the associated reaction pathways (Fig.  5 a). Structurally, GB-RuO 2  is composed of densely interconnected ultrasmall nanoparticles, forming a 2D porous nanosheet architecture with a high density of grain boundaries (Fig.  5 b). Electrochemically, GB-RuO 2  delivers remarkable acidic OER activity in 0.1 M HClO 4 , requiring an overpotential of only 187 mV to reach a current density of 10 mA cm − 2  (Fig.  5 c). In addition, the small Tafel slope of 34.5 mV dec − 1 , together with stable operation exceeding 550 h, highlights the superior reaction kinetics and durability enabled by grain-boundary engineering (Fig.  5 d). To realize rapid and controllable phase modulation in strongly correlated oxides, unconventional strategies capable of driving materials into nonequilibrium states are increasingly sought. Wu et al. implemented a strongly nonequilibrium microwave-shock method to modulate the crystalline phase of porous 2D LaNiO 3  within seconds, enabling precise tuning of structural and electronic configurations [ 149 ]. Notably, this approach preserves the intrinsic porous 2D architecture while successfully stabilizing a highly symmetric cubic phase. The cubic LaNiO 3  phase adopts an ideal perovskite lattice with high structural symmetry and an open framework, which effectively optimizes the geometry of NiO 6  octahedra and enhances Ni 3d–O 2p orbital hybridization, thereby facilitating charge transport and multi-electron reaction kinetics (Fig.  5 e). The material manifests as ultrathin porous nanosheets, providing a large accessible surface area and a high density of exposed active sites (Fig.  5 f). Electrochemical measurements show that cubic LaNiO 3  achieves a low UOR onset potential of ~ 1.27–1.28 V, indicating its high catalytic activity (Fig.  5 g). Moreover, the small Tafel slope of 33.1 mV dec⁻¹ reflects favorable reaction kinetics and efficient charge-transfer behavior (Fig.  5 h). In this context, the performance gap between porous 2D oxides and sulfides for UOR mainly stems from a balance between stability and conductivity. Oxide-based catalysts typically retain stronger structural integrity and more stable surface hydroxyl environments, but their slower electron transport can limit turnover at high current densities. Sulfide-based catalysts, in contrast, usually respond more quickly in UOR because of their higher conductivity and more adaptable surface chemistry, although this advantage must be weighed against their greater susceptibility to oxidation under anodic bias.

Beyond defect and phase control, compositional and structural engineering further expands the catalytic versatility of porous 2D metal oxides. By precisely regulating the pyrolysis of a Ni-BDC-NH 2  metal–organic framework precursor, Shih et al. rationally constructed a 2D NiO/Ni–carbon nanosheet electrocatalyst [ 186 ]. This design effectively addresses the intrinsic limitations in activity and selectivity encountered during the electrochemical AOR. The resulting MOF-derived architecture consists of mesoporous carbon nanoflakes uniformly embedding Ni/NiO core–shell nanoparticles, which collectively afford an enlarged electrochemically active surface area and accelerated charge-transfer kinetics (Fig.  5 i). Electrochemical and spectroscopic analyses reveal that the reversible solid-state Ni 2+ /Ni 3+  redox transition mediates AOR at a substantially lower onset potential than the competing OER, thereby enhancing N 2  selectivity and Faradaic efficiency under alkaline conditions (Fig.  5 j). Notably, the catalyst exhibits sustained performance in a continuous-flow electrolyzer for the treatment of real ammonia-containing wastewater, underscoring its practical applicability and durability (Fig.  5 k). To explore high-entropy strategies in electrocatalyst design, Wang et al. developed single-crystalline mesoporous high-entropy oxides (SC-MHEOs) that integrate ordered lattice frameworks, tunable multicomponent composition, and extensive surface area, collectively enabling superior OER performance [ 188 ]. These materials can be synthesized via a template-free thermal conversion of high-entropy carbonate precursors, yielding 2D nanoplates with penetrated mesoporosity that preserves crystallinity while maximizing mass transport and site accessibility (Fig.  5 l). The high-entropy composition induces lattice distortions and electronic structure modulation, which, in concert with the single-crystalline mesoporous architecture, lowers the activation energies and energy barriers of key intermediates in 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) electrooxidation (Fig.  5 m). Consequently, SC-MHEOs exhibit enhanced reaction kinetics, superior FDCA selectivity, and excellent stability, demonstrating their potential as efficient electrocatalysts for biomass upgrading and other sustainable energy applications (Fig.  5 n).

sections.heading: Porous 2D metal hydroxides
paragraphs: Porous 2D metal hydroxides have garnered significant attention as electrocatalysts for small-molecule oxidation due to their distinctive electronic properties, redox-active sites, and strong hydroxyl-mediated reaction pathways [ 199 ,  200 ]. Unlike other 2D materials, metal hydroxides inherently facilitate proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) through their abundant hydroxyl groups, enhancing charge transport and intermediate stabilization [ 201 ]. The presence of surface-coordinated hydroxyl species promotes efficient reactant adsorption and activation, particularly in OER and alcohol oxidation, where hydroxyl-mediated mechanisms dictate catalytic performance. Moreover, the layered structure of metal hydroxides undergoes dynamic transformations under oxidative conditions, forming highly active oxyhydroxide phases that introduce additional defect sites and optimize catalytic energetics [ 202 ]. Transition metal hydroxides such as Ni(OH) 2 , Co(OH) 2 , and Fe(OH) 3  exhibit flexible oxidation states, enabling continuous redox cycles that drive multi-step oxidation reactions [ 203 ]. Compared to oxides and carbides, metal hydroxides display moderate binding affinities for oxygen-containing intermediates, facilitating efficient product desorption while mitigating catalyst deactivation [ 204 ]. Additionally, their hydrated surface environment plays a crucial role in stabilizing intermediates and modulating reaction kinetics in aqueous electrooxidation systems [ 205 ]. These combined attributes render porous 2D metal hydroxides highly effective for small-molecule oxidation, offering a synergistic balance of tunable active sites, rapid charge transport, and self-regenerating catalytic surfaces that enhance efficiency, selectivity, and long-term stability [ 206 ].

The sluggish reaction kinetics of the OER continue to represent a major bottleneck in water-splitting electrocatalysis, particularly under acidic conditions where catalyst degradation is often exacerbated. To address this challenge, Zheng et al. developed a hybrid catalyst system by partially transforming FeNi layered double hydroxides (FeNi-LDHs) into a 2D/1D FeNi-LDH/metal-organic framework (MOF) architecture through in situ synthesis [ 158 ]. This process yields a hierarchical architecture composed of ultrathin nanosheets (~ 1.34 nm) integrated with 1D, sword-like MOF nanorods with lengths of approximately 1.3 μm (Fig.  6 a). This hierarchical structure maximizes the exposure of active sites and facilitates efficient charge and mass transport. The optimized FeNi-LDH/MOF delivers a low OER overpotential of 272 mV at a current density of 100 mA cm − 2  in alkaline media (Fig.  6 b). It also exhibits favorable reaction kinetics, as reflected by a small Tafel slope of 34.1 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  6 c). In addition, the catalyst maintains high current density and excellent long-term operational stability during continuous OER testing (Fig.  6 d). Beyond hierarchical hybridization strategies, morphology- and composition-directed engineering of layered double hydroxides has further been demonstrated to effectively tailor active site chemistry and boost electrocatalytic oxidation performance. Zhu et al. developed an optimized hydrothermal method to fabricate NiMn- and NiFe-layered double hydroxide nanosheet arrays uniformly anchored on nickel foam, achieving well-defined architectures with improved active site exposure and interfacial contact [ 28 ]. Structural characterization by X-ray diffraction and high-resolution TEM confirms layered hexagonal phases with well-defined lattice parameters and high crystallinity (Fig.  6 e). The catalysts exhibit a 2D porous architecture, providing large surface area and homogeneous distribution of metal cations (Fig.  6 f). Electrochemical tests show that NiMn-LDH achieves low cell potentials of 1.33 and 1.41 V at 10 and 100 mA cm − 2 , respectively, with nearly 100% Faradaic efficiency in methanol-to-formate oxidation (Fig.  6 g). The catalyst also exhibits favorable reaction kinetics, reflected by a Tafel slope of 39.4 mV dec − 1 , along with robust stability in alkaline media (Fig.  6 h).

Building on these LDH strategies, interface engineering and heteroatom modulation have been shown to further enhance active sites and catalytic performance. Feng et al. engineered a hybrid electrocatalyst by decorating cobalt–nickel layered double hydroxide (LDH) nanosheets with fullerene quantum dots (FQDs), thereby enhancing active site exposure and modulating interfacial charge transfer dynamics [ 179 ]. Through a facile self-assembly process, the composite was firmly anchored onto porous nickel foam, yielding a structurally integrated electrocatalytic platform. The FQD/CoNi-LDH/NF composite exhibits a 2D nanosheet architecture with uniform integration of fullerene quantum dots (Fig.  6 i). Its porous structure provides a high specific surface area of 32.07 m 2  g − 2 , facilitating enhanced active site exposure and mass transport (Fig.  6 j). The catalyst reaches a current density of 10 mA cm − 2  at 1.36 V versus RHE, with a Tafel slope of 17 mV dec − 1 , outperforming CoNi-LDH/NF and commercial IrO 2 /NF (Fig.  6 k). It also demonstrates excellent long-term operational stability under continuous testing (Fig.  6 l). The superior performance is ascribed to synergistic charge transfer from FQDs to CoNi-LDH and the structural advantages of the porous nanosheets, highlighting its potential as a high-performance, multifunctional electrocatalyst. Despite recent progress in HMF electrooxidation, Ni-based catalysts remain limited by sluggish reaction kinetics and inadequate active site utilization. To address these challenges, Wang et al. designed an interdisciplinary strategy to overcome intrinsic kinetic bottlenecks by constructing a tailored Ni-based electrocatalyst architecture optimized for enhanced adsorption dynamics and electron transfer efficiency during HMF oxidation [ 189 ]. To this end, a dual-dopant electronic modulation strategy was implemented by the simultaneous incorporation of boron and manganese into ultrathin Ni(OH) 2  nanosheets. The electron-deficient boron dopant serves as an effective electron sink, inducing charge transfer from Ni centers and stabilizing higher Ni oxidation states, thereby substantially lowering the energy barrier for catalyst dehydrogenation (Fig.  6 m). Meanwhile, the resulting material adopts an interconnected 2D nanosheet morphology with a thickness of approximately 0.47 nm, approaching the theoretical monolayer limit and enabling abundant exposure of active sites as well as accelerated mass and charge transport (Fig.  6 n). As a consequence of the synergistic electronic and structural advantages, the B–NiMn(OH) 2  catalyst demonstrates excellent electrochemical kinetics, achieving an ultra-low onset potential of 1.30 V and reaching 100 mA·cm − 2  at 1.36 V, with a low Tafel slope of 18.9 mV·dec − 1 (Fig.  6 o). In addition, it exhibits nearly complete HMF conversion, a high FDCA yield of 99.2%, and a Faradaic efficiency of 97.2%, ranking among the most efficient noble-metal-free catalysts for HMF electrooxidation (Fig.  6 p).

sections.heading: Porous 2D metal sulfides
paragraphs: Porous 2D metal sulfides have emerged as highly effective electrocatalysts for small-molecule oxidation due to their distinctive electronic structures, tunable surface chemistry, and optimized intermediate adsorption properties [ 207 ]. Unlike oxides and hydroxides, metal sulfides exhibit enhanced covalency in metal–sulfur bonds and lower electronegativity, which facilitate charge delocalization and reduce the energy barrier for electron transfer. The intrinsic p-d hybridization between sulfur and transition metals modulates the adsorption strength of key oxidation intermediates, preventing excessive binding of *OH, *COO, or *O species that could otherwise lead to surface poisoning and hinder catalytic turnover [ 208 ]. Additionally, metal sulfides generally exhibit higher intrinsic conductivity than oxides, enabling more efficient charge transport in multi-electron oxidation reactions where slow electron mobility often limits catalytic efficiency. Another crucial advantage of metal sulfides is their in situ surface reconstruction under oxidative conditions, which leads to the formation of oxy-sulfide or hydroxylated species, expanding the diversity of active sites and enhancing reaction kinetics [ 209 ]. The relatively weaker M–S bond strength compared to M–O bonds also facilitates the formation of sulfur vacancies, which serve as preferential adsorption centers that reduce activation barriers and enhance reactivity [ 210 ]. These vacancies contribute to improved reactant adsorption while simultaneously tuning the electronic structure to optimize charge transfer and catalytic performance. Given these distinct properties, porous 2D metal sulfides offer a synergistic combination of high charge transport efficiency, adaptive surface reactivity, and finely tuned intermediate binding, making them highly promising catalysts for small-molecule oxidation with superior activity, selectivity, and stability [ 211 ].

Given the sluggish kinetics of the OER and the difficulty in steering surface reconstruction in nickel-based systems, advanced structural design strategies have become essential. Zhao et al. addressed this challenge by constructing an ultrathin and porous Ni 3 S 2 /NiO nanomesh via a one-step hydrothermal method, achieving enhanced exposure of active sites and improved catalytic dynamics [ 165 ]. The material adopts a 2D nanomesh architecture with an ultrathin thickness of approximately 3 nm (Fig.  7 a). Its abundant in-plane nanopores and edge-rich Ni 3 S 2 /NiO heterointerfaces provide numerous active sites, promote hydroxide adsorption, and facilitate mass and charge transport during the OER (Fig.  7 b). As a result, the Ni 3 S 2 /NiO nanomeshes achieve a low OER overpotential of 300 mV at a current density of 200 mA cm − 2  in alkaline media (Fig.  7 c). They also exhibit favorable reaction kinetics, with a small Tafel slope of 32 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  7 d). In addition, the catalyst maintains stable operation at 200 mA cm − 2  for at least 12 h. Building on these porous 2D architectures, further structural and electronic engineering has been shown to enhance catalytic activity and stability for alcohol oxidation reactions. He et al. developed a grain-boundary engineering strategy to construct ultrathin porous RuO 2  nanosheets with abundant grain boundaries (GB-RuO 2 ), employing a salt-assisted recrystallization method to improve acidic OER stability [ 177 ]. In particular, Cr doping was employed to tailor the electronic structure of Ni 3 S 2 , thereby promoting its intrinsic MOR activity. The resulting Cr–Ni 3 S 2  catalyst features a 2D interconnected porous nanosheet architecture, which maximizes the exposure of catalytically active sites and facilitates efficient mass transport, thus favoring MOR kinetics (Fig.  7 e, f). Benefiting from the synergistic effects of structural and electronic modulation, Cr–Ni 3 S 2  exhibits outstanding MOR performance, delivering a low anodic potential of 1.36 V vs. RHE at 10 mA cm − 2  in 0.1 M methanol, along with a small Tafel slope of 46.4 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  7 g). Furthermore, the catalyst demonstrates stable operation over extended electrolysis, highlighting its robust electrochemical durability under MOR conditions (Fig.  7 h).

Building on these 2D design strategies, similar approaches have been applied to enhance urea and alcohol electrooxidation. Hu et al. have developed a bimetallic Fe–Ni sulfide cluster supported on defect-rich ultrathin hexagonal boron nitride nanosheets (FNS/d-B) through theory-guided synthesis to enhance electrocatalytic performance [ 180 ]. The material exhibits a well-defined crystalline sulfide phase with abundant unsaturated coordination sites, providing a high density of active centers (Fig.  7 i). Its 2D porous architecture ensures uniform cluster dispersion, facilitates mass transport, and promotes rapid electron transfer, thereby effectively accelerating the UOR (Fig.  7 j). Consequently, FNS/d-B exhibits favorable reaction kinetics with a Tafel slope of 50.41 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  7 k). It also demonstrates high electrocatalytic efficiency, achieving nitrite selectivity above 80% and a Faradaic efficiency exceeding 95%, markedly outperforming BN, d-BNNS, and conventional catalysts (Fig.  7 l). As part of ongoing efforts to enhance urea electrooxidation activity through interfacial electronic modulation, Du et al. constructed a CoS 1.097 /Ni 3 S 2  heterojunction using a one-step hydrothermal synthesis method. This heterostructure was designed to leverage built-in electric fields at the interface to accelerate charge transfer and optimize urea adsorption kinetics [ 182 ]. The catalyst adopts a 2D porous nanosheet architecture, which offers abundant active sites and facilitates charge transfer, thereby promoting urea adsorption and accelerating reaction kinetics (Fig.  7 m). The CoS 1.097 /Ni 3 S 2  heterostructure reaches 100 mA cm − 2  at 1.22 V vs. RHE, corresponding to an overpotential of 0.85 V (Fig.  7 n). It maintains long-term stability at high current densities during continuous UOR testing (Fig.  7 o). The catalyst also exhibits favorable kinetics, with a Tafel slope of 33.43 mV dec − 1 , outperforming single-component CoS 1.097  or Ni 3 S 2  (Fig.  7 p).

sections.heading: Porous 2D metal phosphides
paragraphs: Porous 2D metal phosphides have gained significant attention as electrocatalysts for small-molecule oxidation due to their distinct electronic properties, covalent metal–phosphorus bonding, and intrinsic conductivity, which set them apart from oxides, hydroxides, and sulfides. Unlike metal oxides and hydroxides, which rely on ionic interactions and localized charge distributions, metal phosphides exhibit delocalized electronic states that enhance charge transport and catalytic stability under oxidative conditions. Their optimized d-band structure facilitates efficient reactant activation by modulating adsorption energies and electron transfer kinetics [ 212 ]. The moderate electronegativity of phosphorus further tunes the coordination environment of metal centers, reducing excessive oxygen affinity and preventing catalyst deactivation, a common issue in oxide-based systems [ 213 ]. This feature is particularly beneficial in alcohol and UOR, where controlled intermediate desorption is crucial for minimizing surface poisoning effects. Additionally, phosphorus incorporation induces electronic asymmetry and surface polarity variations, promoting the stabilization of oxidation intermediates such as *OH, *O, and *CO, thereby improving catalytic efficiency [ 214 ]. The inherent hydrophobicity of many metal phosphides also influences interfacial interactions, selectively adsorbing organic reactants while suppressing unwanted side reactions in aqueous systems [ 215 ]. Furthermore, these materials undergo electrochemical restructuring under operational conditions, forming mixed-valence oxyphosphide phases that exhibit enhanced catalytic activity compared to their pristine counterparts [ 216 ]. This dynamic evolution increases active site accessibility and introduces reactive defect states that accelerate oxidation kinetics. The combined advantages of electronic tunability, structural adaptability, and oxidation resistance make porous 2D metal phosphides a highly effective platform for small-molecule oxidation, offering superior activity, selectivity, and long-term durability [ 217 ].

In the pursuit of robust and efficient OER electrocatalysts, transition metal phosphides have garnered attention due to their favorable electronic conductivity and tunable active sites. Li et al. developed Fe-doped Ni 2 P nanosheets coated with a conformal carbon layer on nickel foam (Fe-Ni 2 P@C/NF), effectively enhancing catalytic performance by simultaneously optimizing charge transfer and surface stability [ 169 ]. The Fe dopants modulate the electronic structure of Ni 2 P, while the carbon coating improves electrical conductivity. The material adopts a 2D porous nanosheet architecture, offering a high surface area and abundant active sites that facilitate both mass transport and electron transfer during OER (Fig.  8 a). As a result, Fe-Ni 2 P@C/NF achieves current densities of 200 and 400 mA cm − 2  at overpotentials of 255 and 269 mV, respectively (Fig.  8 b). The catalyst maintains excellent structural stability during extended operation (Fig.  8 c). It also exhibits favorable reaction kinetics, with a low Tafel slope of 64 mV dec − 1 , outperforming Fe-Ni 2 P/NF, Ni 2 P@C/NF, and commercial IrO 2 . (Fig.  8 d). Building upon prior advances in seawater electrooxidation catalysis, efforts have increasingly focused on compositional modulation to enhance catalytic activity and corrosion resistance under alkaline marine conditions. Li et al. developed a Ru-doped Ni 2 P/Fe 2 P nanosheet system via a solvothermal approach followed by low-temperature phosphidation, achieving improved electrocatalytic performance in alkaline seawater oxidation [ 170 ]. The vertically staggered Ni 2 P/Fe 2 P heterojunction exposes Ni and Fe (111) facets, optimizing electron distribution and lowering the OER energy barrier (Fig.  8 e). Its 2D porous architecture significantly increases the electrochemically active surface area, facilitates electrolyte infiltration, and accelerates gas release, collectively promoting OER efficiency (Fig.  8 f). Consequently, the catalyst exhibits favorable reaction kinetics, with a Tafel slope of 71.0 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  8 g). It also achieves an overpotential of 331 mV at 1000 mA cm − 2 , demonstrating robust performance under high-current seawater electrolysis conditions (Fig.  8 h).

To enhance the energy efficiency of hydrogen production, researchers have increasingly turned to multifunctional catalyst architectures that integrate redox-active interfaces with high-conductivity backbones [ 218 ]. Qiao et al. constructed a heterostructured electrocatalyst by coupling crystalline–amorphous nickel–cobalt phosphides with phosphorus-doped manganese oxides (c-CoNiP x /a-P-MnO y ), synthesized through a controlled phosphorization strategy [ 183 ]. The material exhibits a hierarchical, 2D porous architecture that enhances exposure of active sites, facilitates reactant adsorption, and promotes electron transfer, thereby optimizing UOR kinetics (Fig.  8 i). Compared with the OER, UOR proceeds at significantly lower potentials, offering substantial energy savings (Fig.  8 j). Under 1 M KOH with 0.5 M urea, c-CoNiP x /a-P-MnO y  reaches current densities of 10 and 100 mA cm − 2  at 1.24 and 1.35 V vs. (Fig.  8 k). RHE, respectively. The catalyst exhibits favorable reaction kinetics, with a Tafel slope of 75 mV dec − 1 , surpassing CoNiP x /MnO and MnCoNiO m  analogs (Fig.  8 l). Given the sluggish kinetics and poor selectivity of conventional catalysts toward HzOR, targeted heteroatomic modulation has emerged as a promising strategy to optimize surface reactivity. Meng et al. introduced [W–O] species into CoP nanoflakes through an in situ hydrolysis etching route, thereby constructing a heterostructure that significantly enhances the HzOR [ 151 ]. The resulting material retains an orthorhombic CoP structure with uniformly doped W and O atoms (Fig.  8 m) and simultaneously develops a 2D porous architecture, which increases active site exposure and facilitates mass transport (Fig.  8 n). The 6 W–O–CoP/NF catalyst exhibits exceptionally fast reaction kinetics, as evidenced by a low Tafel slope of 8.43 mV dec − 1 , suggesting a nearly complete four-electron oxidation pathway (Fig.  8 o). It also delivers an ultra-low overpotential of 78.99 mV at a high current density of 1000 mA cm − 2 , reflecting markedly accelerated HzOR kinetics (Fig.  8 p). The combined effects of enhanced adsorption, porous morphology, and electronic tuning account for the catalyst’s superior performance in HzOR.

sections.heading: Porous 2D metal carbides and nitrides
paragraphs: Porous 2D metal carbides and nitrides, particularly MXenes and related transition metal-based compounds, have attracted significant attention as electrocatalysts for small-molecule oxidation due to their unique combination of high electrical conductivity, tunable surface chemistry, and excellent structural stability under oxidative conditions. Unlike metal oxides and hydroxides, which rely primarily on redox-active sites, carbides and nitrides exhibit intrinsic metallic conductivity, enabling rapid charge transfer that reduces overpotential losses and accelerates reaction kinetics [ 219 ,  220 ]. This advantage is particularly crucial in oxidation reactions where sluggish electron transport limits catalytic efficiency, such as FAOR. Additionally, their moderate binding affinities for reaction intermediates provide an optimal balance between adsorption strength and catalytic turnover, preventing catalyst poisoning while maintaining efficient reaction progression [ 221 ]. Unlike noble metals with excessively strong adsorption or oxides with high desorption barriers, carbides and nitrides stabilize key intermediates without excessive accumulation, optimizing oxidation energetics. The surface termination groups (e.g., -OH, -O, -F) in MXenes further regulate adsorption behavior, dynamically modulating oxidation pathways [ 222 ]. Moreover, the strong covalent bonding in metal carbides and nitrides ensures high structural resilience, preventing dissolution and phase degradation under oxidative conditions—common challenges faced by oxides and hydroxides. Their porous architecture and atomic-layer thickness further enhance catalytic performance by exposing a high density of active sites and facilitating efficient mass transport, particularly in multi-step oxidation reactions where rapid intermediate diffusion is essential. These synergistic properties render porous 2D metal carbides and nitrides exceptionally effective for small-molecule oxidation, providing a combination of fast charge transfer, optimized intermediate adsorption, and superior long-term durability, thereby improving both catalytic activity and selectivity [ 223 ].

Given the synthetic and structural difficulties posed by 2D nonlayered heterostructures, bottom-up fabrication methods have gained increasing attention for overcoming lattice mismatch and interfacial instability. Kou et al. implemented such a strategy by constructing 2D nonlayered heterostructures through a controlled bottom-up synthesis route, enabling precise modulation of heterointerfaces and enhanced structural coherence [ 172 ]. This approach involved the thermal annealing of Mo/Zn bimetallic imidazolate frameworks to fabricate holey 2D Mo 2 C/Mo 2 N heterostructured nanosheets with controlled morphology and architecture. The resulting interconnected and highly porous 2D architecture, featuring chemically integrated Mo 2 C–Mo 2 N microdomains, effectively increases the density of exposed active sites, creates abundant N–Mo–C interfacial motifs, and facilitates charge transport, thereby promoting OER kinetics (Fig.  9 a, b). Owing to these structural advantages, the h-TMCN catalyst achieves a low OER overpotential of approximately 276 mV at a current density of 50 mA cm − 2 , outperforming both dense counterparts and benchmark RuO 2  (Fig.  9 c). It also exhibits favorable reaction kinetics, as reflected by a reduced Tafel slope of 82 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  9 d). Building upon the growing interest in heterostructure engineering to enhance electrocatalytic UOR, researchers have begun integrating multiple metal nitride phases to synergistically tune surface activity and electronic coupling. Wang et al. designed and synthesized a Ni 3 N/Mo 2 N heterostructured electrocatalyst through a hydrothermal route, achieving intimate phase interfacing that facilitates charge redistribution and improved urea adsorption kinetics [ 184 ]. Through controlled nitridation, the material effectively lowered the anodic energy barrier for water electrolysis, thereby substituting the kinetically sluggish OER with the more energetically favorable UOR. The catalyst comprises hexagonal Ni 3 N and Mo 2 N phases, whose low-symmetry heterointerfaces induce pronounced interfacial charge redistribution, effectively modulating the adsorption of UOR-relevant intermediates (Fig.  9 e). Its 2D porous nanosheet morphology provides a high density of exposed active sites and facilitates efficient charge and mass transport, thereby promoting urea adsorption and accelerating reaction kinetics (Fig.  9 f). Electrochemical measurements reveal that the Ni 3 N/Mo 2 N catalyst exhibits a pronounced advantage for UOR over OER, with the operating potential at 200 mA cm − 2  being 328 mV lower and the UOR current density at 1.40 V reaching 6.1 and 2.4 times those of Ni 3 N and Mo 2 N, respectively (Fig.  9 g). Moreover, the catalyst delivers a current density of 10 mA cm − 2  at an applied potential of 1.36 V, reflecting its favorable overpotential performance (Fig.  9 h).

To explore multifunctional electrocatalysts that integrate noble metals with transition metal nitrides, recent efforts have focused on tailoring hybrid interfaces at the nanoscale. Chen et al. employed a hydrothermal synthesis strategy to construct Ir–Ni 3 N nanosheets featuring atomically coupled heterointerfaces between metallic Ir and conductive Ni 3 N domains [ 185 ]. Subsequent high-temperature calcination was applied to optimize their structural and electronic properties, thereby significantly enhancing hydrogen production from urea-containing wastewater. The material adopts a hexagonal Ni 3 N crystal structure (Fig.  9 i) with well-defined lattice fringes and ordered symmetry, as revealed by HRTEM and SAED analyses (Fig.  9 j). Its 2D porous nanosheet architecture provides abundant active sites and facilitates rapid mass transport, thereby promoting efficient urea adsorption and oxidation. The catalyst exhibits a clear thermodynamic advantage for UOR over OER, delivering a current density of 100 mA cm − 2  at 1.37 V vs. RHE, which is 220 mV lower than the potential required for OER (1.59 V) (Fig.  9 k). It also shows favorable reaction kinetics, as evidenced by a small Tafel slope of 27.73 mV dec − 1 , indicating superior intrinsic activity (Fig.  9 l). To enhance the structural and electronic properties of Ni 3 N-based electrocatalysts, compositional modulation strategies have been actively explored. Zhao et al. implemented a Cu substitution strategy by nitriding a Ni–Cu precursor, thereby synthesizing antiperovskite Ni 3 CuN nanosheets with modified electronic structures and lattice configurations [ 187 ]. The resulting 2D porous nanosheet structure provides a high surface area and abundant active sites, promoting efficient mass transport and electron transfer during benzylamine oxidation (Fig.  9 m, n). Specifically, Ni 3 CuN delivers high electrocatalytic activity, achieving a current density twice that of Ni 3 N at an applied potential of 1.45 V vs. RHE (Fig.  9 o). It also exhibits faster reaction kinetics, as evidenced by a low Tafel slope of 26.1 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  9 p). Moreover, the catalyst maintains a high Faradaic efficiency of approximately 95%, indicating excellent selectivity and durability. The catalyst also demonstrates broad applicability, converting 4-fluorobenzylamine and tetrahydroisoquinoline with 90% and 82%.
