sections.heading: Other emerging porous 2D materials
paragraphs: Beyond the porous 2D metal oxides, hydroxides, sulfides, phosphides, and carbides or nitrides discussed above, a growing body of evidence demonstrates that a broader spectrum of emerging porous 2D materials can also deliver exceptional performance in electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation, owing to their unconventional electronic structures and interfacial chemistry [ 224 ]. These systems include porous 2D carbon-based single-atom frameworks, mesoporous noble-metal nanosheets, 2D metal nanowire networks, and complex multicomponent nanosheet assemblies, all of which deviate from classical crystalline lattices yet exhibit highly optimized structure–activity relationships. In such materials, the porous 2D geometry not only maximizes the exposure of low-coordination sites but also enables precise spatial arrangement of heteroatoms, single-metal centers, or multimetallic ensembles, thereby allowing cooperative adsorption and activation of key intermediates such as OH ads , CO-like species, or N–H and C–C bonds [ 225 ]. The combination of atomic-scale active motifs with extended 2D electron transport pathways promotes rapid charge redistribution and lowers kinetic barriers for bond cleavage steps that are typically rate-limiting in small-molecule oxidation. Moreover, the presence of grain boundaries, lattice distortions, and anisotropic pore architectures introduces locally heterogeneous electronic environments, which can selectively stabilize reactive intermediates while suppressing poisoning pathways [ 226 ]. From a broader perspective, emerging porous 2D platforms such as metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) further expand this design space by offering programmable coordination environments, long-range order, and tunable redox-active nodes, enabling rational control over adsorption energetics and reaction selectivity. Collectively, these emerging porous 2D materials highlight that catalytic superiority in small-molecule electrooxidation arises not from porosity or dimensionality alone, but from the synergistic coupling of confined 2D architectures with tailored electronic and chemical heterogeneity, which together redefine the achievable limits of activity, selectivity, and stability [ 225 ].

Given the intrinsically sluggish kinetics of the OER under harsh electrochemical conditions, developing catalysts with maximized atomic utilization and synergistic redox centers remains a critical challenge. Cui et al. addressed this issue by constructing an iron–manganese dual single-atom catalyst, wherein spatially isolated Fe and Mn sites cooperatively modulate intermediate adsorption and reaction energetics [ 173 ]. Using a molten-salt–assisted pyrolysis approach, adjacent Fe–N 4  and Mn–N 4  sites were precisely anchored on ultrathin, porous nitrogen-doped carbon nanosheets, enabling a structurally well-defined and highly active electrocatalytic system. FeMn-DSAC features an ultrathin two-dimensional nanosheet structure with micrometer-scale lateral size and ~ 3.0 nm thickness, enabled by eutectic-salt-assisted pyrolysis (Fig.  10 a). Its hierarchical micro/mesoporous architecture affords a high surface area (1700 m 2  g − 1 ) and large pore volume (0.95 cm 3  g − 1 ), facilitating efficient active-site exposure and mass transport. (Fig.  10 b). Owing to the synergistic interaction between neighboring Fe and Mn centers and the structural advantages of the ultrathin nanosheets, the catalyst exhibits markedly improved OER performance in alkaline media, achieving a current density of 10 mA cm − 2  at an overpotential of 405 mV (Fig.  10 c). In addition, a relatively small Tafel slope of 96 mV dec − 1  is obtained, indicative of accelerated OER kinetics compared with the corresponding single-atom catalysts and bulk-structured counterparts, and approaching the activity of state-of-the-art noble-metal-based catalysts (Fig.  10 d). Building on these strategies, the design of ultrathin, porous two-dimensional nanosheets with precisely engineered active sites has emerged as a powerful approach to enhance electrocatalytic performance across diverse reactions. Fan et al. have developed anisotropic 2D PtRhPb mesoporous nanosheets through a surfactant-free selective etching strategy to address the intrinsically low activity and limited C1 selectivity of alkaline EOR.[228] The resulting 2D mesoporous framework, characterized by uniformly distributed 2–4 nm pores, thin pore walls, exposed (110) facets, and abundant low-coordinated metal sites, effectively stabilizes OH ads  intermediates and enables synergistic Pt–Rh interactions that facilitate C–C bond cleavage (Fig.  10 e, f). The alkaline ethanol oxidation reaction (EOR) performance of the catalysts was assessed in N 2 -saturated 1.0 M KOH containing 1.0 M ethanol, with polarization curves showing broad anodic peaks corresponding to ethanol oxidation and sharp cathodic features associated with the removal of adsorbed intermediates (CH 3 CO a d s  and CO a d s ) (Fig.  10 g). Among the tested materials, anisotropic PtRhPb mesoporous nanosheets demonstrated superior activity, achieving a mass activity of 7.8 A mg NM −1  at 0.23 V, significantly outperforming PtPb nanosheets (4.3 A mg NM −1 , 0.48 V), PtRhPb nanoparticles (4.7 A mg NM −1 ,0.48 V), and Pt nanoparticles (1.2 A mg NM −1 , 0.52 V) (Fig.  10 h).

To harness the structural advantages of 2D architectures in metal nanowire-based electrocatalysis, precise control over nanowire assembly and spatial arrangement is essential. Zhang et al. devised a microfluidic laminar-flow strategy that enables confined in-plane growth of 2D metal nanowire networks by leveraging spatial restriction and directional shear forces [ 150 ]. This strategy enables the direct fabrication of extensive, continuous alloy networks with controlled morphology. The resulting 2D porous architecture of interconnected ultrathin nanowires promotes active site exposure and efficient electron transport, thereby facilitating FAOR (Fig.  10 i). PdBi-2D MNWNs exhibit a superior mass activity of 2669.1 mA mg − 1  at ~ 0.2 V, substantially higher than other Pd-based catalysts (Fig.  10 j). The catalyst possesses an electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) of 11.0 m 2  g − 1 , higher than that of entangled MNWNs (Fig.  10 k). Chronoamperometric measurements confirm that the 2D structure provides excellent stability, maintaining high activity during prolonged operation (Fig.  10 l). Inspired by advances in light-driven synthetic strategies for complex nanostructures, researchers have sought to leverage photo-induced pathways to construct multimetallic architectures with tailored porosity. Zhao et al. independently developed a visible-light-triggered Bi 2 Te 3 -mediated route to synthesize ultrathin porous PtBiTe and PtAgBiTe nanosheets, effectively integrating multiple active sites within a 2D framework [ 190 ]. These nanosheets, composed of sub-5 nm grains, form polycrystalline 2D porous architectures with abundant grain boundaries, low-coordination edge sites, and lattice distortions, which enhance hydrazine adsorption and facilitate N–H bond activation during oxidation (Fig.  10 m, n). As a result, PtAgBiTe nanosheets demonstrate excellent electrocatalytic kinetics for HzOR, with a low Tafel slope of 13.9 mV dec − 1  (Fig.  10 o). They also exhibit a high mass activity of 13.5 A mg −1 Pt  and a turnover frequency of 6.82 s − 1  at 100 mV, significantly surpassing PtBiTe nanosheets and commercial Pt/C catalysts. (Fig.  10 p).

sections.heading: Summary, challenges, and perspectives
paragraphs: Porous 2D materials have demonstrated exceptional potential for electrocatalytic small-molecule oxidation by integrating high surface area, tunable active sites, and efficient charge transport pathways. This review provides a structure-centric perspective, systematically analyzing how pore engineering, defect modulation, and electronic structure tuning directly influence oxidation reaction kinetics and selectivity. Unlike prior studies that primarily classify catalysts based on composition, this work emphasizes the intricate structure–activity relationships that govern oxidation mechanisms, highlighting how in situ transformations and dynamic electronic reconfigurations enhance catalytic efficiency. By bridging fundamental material properties with electrochemical performance, this review establishes a rational design strategy for optimizing porous 2D electrocatalysts, moving beyond empirical approaches to guide the next generation of oxidation catalysts with improved activity, selectivity, and long-term stability.

Despite these advancements, several critical challenges remain, requiring a deeper understanding of catalyst behavior during operation. One key challenge lies in the dynamic restructuring of active sites and electronic states during oxidation reactions, particularly for materials that undergo oxidation-state transitions or phase transformations under applied potential. While such changes can enhance catalytic activity by exposing metastable reactive phases, they also introduce uncertainties in structural reversibility, active site retention, and long-term stability. Understanding the kinetics and thermodynamics governing these transformations is essential for designing catalysts with controlled adaptability rather than unpredictable degradation. Another major challenge is establishing a precise correlation between local electronic environments and oxidation reaction energetics. While previous studies have shown the influence of defect sites, heteroatom doping, and charge redistribution on intermediate adsorption, the quantitative relationship between charge density variations and oxidation selectivity remains insufficiently understood. This limitation hinders the rational design of catalysts capable of steering oxidation reactions toward preferred products while suppressing side reactions. Furthermore, the scalability and integration of porous 2D electrocatalysts into functional electrochemical systems remain significant obstacles. Although these materials exhibit high intrinsic activity, their mechanical stability, electrode compatibility, and performance under industrially relevant current densities require further optimization. Developing scalable synthesis routes for porous 2D electrocatalysts should prioritize not only yield and throughput, but also the preservation of hierarchical pore networks, defect density, phase purity, and interlayer spacing, while suppressing restacking and uncontrolled surface reconstruction. For practical deployment, the synthesis process should be tuned to deliver reproducible transport pathways, stable electrode adhesion, and well-defined site distributions under industrially relevant current densities.

Addressing these challenges requires shifting from conventional catalyst development toward adaptive catalytic systems that dynamically respond to reaction conditions. One promising direction is the design of electrocatalysts with tunable active sites, where external stimuli such as electric fields, light irradiation, or mechanical strain modify surface reactivity in real time, allowing precise control over intermediate binding and oxidation pathways. Such dynamic catalysts could mitigate selectivity issues by adjusting electronic structures in response to different reaction environments, ensuring optimal performance across a broad range of oxidation reactions. Additionally, integrating multi-functional catalytic interfaces within porous 2D frameworks represents a promising strategy for optimizing electrocatalysis. The deliberate combination of distinct active centers, electronic mediators, and defect-engineered interfaces could enhance charge transfer, stabilize intermediates, and prevent catalyst deactivation. Constructing hierarchically structured hybrid materials incorporating conductive supports, chemically distinct catalytic domains, and controlled porosity may enable simultaneous optimization of activity, selectivity, and long-term stability. Moreover, the application of machine learning-driven catalyst design and high-throughput computational screening presents a transformative approach to accelerating material discovery. For porous 2D materials used in small-molecule oxidation, machine-learning models should focus on descriptors that directly encode catalytic reactivity and transport behavior, including the d-band or p-band center, Bader charge, work function, vacancy formation energy, local coordination number, pore-size distribution, tortuosity, and reconstruction energy under anodic bias. Reaction-specific adsorption free energies of key intermediates, such as *OH, *O, and *OOH for OER, *CO, *CHO, and *COOH for alcohol oxidation and FAOR, and *NHx or *N2Hx species for UOR, AOR, and HzOR, should also be included to improve model relevance. In parallel, operando synchrotron XAS, especially metal L-edge and S K-edge XANES/EXAFS, operando Raman spectroscopy, ambient-pressure XPS, and operando ATR-FTIR or SEIRAS are urgently needed to capture the oxidation-state evolution, sulfur–metal bond evolution, and sulfide-to-oxyhydroxide restructuring of porous 2D metal sulfides under working potentials. By leveraging data-driven optimization methods alongside in situ spectroscopic validation, previously unexplored catalyst structures with superior oxidation performance can be identified and refined. As these advanced design paradigms evolve, the development of highly efficient, durable, and industrially scalable porous 2D electrocatalysts for small-molecule oxidation will become increasingly feasible, unlocking new opportunities for energy conversion and sustainable electrochemical oxidation technologies.
